newsitem.title: UK: INSIGHT-Cocoa seen lower on weak technicals.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Cocoa seen lower on weak technicals.

text.p: SEPT Close * Support * Resist * RSI14 * MA10 * MA30
Cocoa futures may drift lower and extend recent losses as London's weakening technical picture provides more ammunition for market bears, technical analysts said on Thursday.
London futures managed to hold slim gains by Wednesday's close, following short-covering buying and a technical rebound to fund-led sales earlier in the week.
But earlier in the week benchmark September sank to a fresh four-month low as fresh selling and more fund long liquidation took their toll on prices.
Short-term momentum indicators remained in negative territory and technical analysts said this week's trough of 968 stg a tonne would act as a crucial bear signal if broken.
"That would start a fall which should extend back to around 920," said Trevor Neil, senior analyst at Union Cal Futures.
Traders called the market to open five stg lower than Wednesday's close.
Cocoa's breakdown point came when September slid through the 995 low scored in early April and closed the runaway gap in mid-March between 989 and 1,010.
"I think cocoa will turn down again," Neil said. "I see yesterday's steady performance as a reaction to cocoa's breakdown point."
Analysts said the psychological 1,000 barrier would also act as a substantial upside hurdle, with the weak technical picture unlikely to change until September regained a footing above that point.
Fundamentally, traders were watching crop development in West Africa but a more complete picture of the likely size of the 1997/98 Ivorian crop would probably not emerge until next month.
Buyers and exporters said Ivory Coast was likely to raise its reference cocoa and coffee farmgate prices in the 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) season.
In its daily report, brokers GNI said that could be positive in the short term as it would encourage holding over a larger portion of the mid-crop to mix it with the new season's main crop beans.
Higher local prices would also encourage farmers to maximise the yield of trees, GNI said.
